blocks.text: Before we can talk about arrays, we need a working picture of where a program keeps its data. Not a precise hardware diagram — a simplified model that is accurate enough to predict what your code will cost. Almost every claim in this course, including why reading `arr[i]` takes the same time no matter how large the array is, follows from this one model.

Start with the smallest interesting thing a computer does: adding two numbers. The CPU holds a handful of tiny slots called registers, and an arithmetic unit that can add the values sitting in them. Feed it 10 and 6 and it produces 16.

blocks.alt: Two numbers, 10 and 6, entering a CPU containing an ALU and registers, and the value 16 coming out
blocks.caption: The CPU can add two numbers and produce the result

blocks.text: But registers number in the dozens, not the millions. The moment the CPU needs that 16 again later — or needs to hold a thousand values at once — it has to put the result somewhere else. That somewhere is main memory, or RAM.

Picture RAM as one enormously long row of numbered slots. Each slot holds a fixed, tiny amount of data — one byte — and each has a permanent number called its **address**. The addresses run in order, with no gaps, from one end of memory to the other.

blocks.alt: A row of memory slots numbered 1000 through 1007, with the value 16 stored in the slot at address 1003
blocks.caption: Every byte of memory has its own address

blocks.text: What the CPU can do with an address
The CPU's conversation with memory is narrower than you might expect. There are only two operations, and both take an address:

items: **Read** — hand memory an address, get back the byte stored there.
**Write** — hand memory an address and a value, and the value replaces whatever was there.

blocks.text: The critical property is that both operations cost the same regardless of **which** address you name. Reading address 1003 is no faster than reading address 4,000,000,003. Memory does not scan from the beginning to find a slot — the address is wired directly to the hardware that holds it, which is exactly why it is called random access memory.

Hold on to two facts: addresses are consecutive integers, and reading any address costs the same. An array is what you get when you take those two facts and lay out a group of same-sized values one after another. Because the values are evenly spaced and the first address is known, the machine can compute the address of any element with a single multiplication and addition, then do one constant-cost read.
That computation — `address = start + index × size` — is the whole reason `arr[i]` is an **O(1)** operation, and the next lesson builds it up step by step.
